Well, see, that’s the thing. It’s... it’s gotten really bad lately. You see, I’ve actually been off the road for a bit. Pleasure? Enjoyment? No, doc, no. Not at all. I mean, you'd think so, right? You'd think if a guy is sitting there eating a whole pizza and a family-sized bag of chips, he must be having the time of his life. But it's not like that. It's... it's almost the opposite.

Honestly, I don't even think I taste the food half the time. It's just... it's just shoveling it in. It's like I'm trying to fill a hole or just numb out the boredom and the frustration of this damn back injury. I'm sitting there, my back is aching, I'm miserable because I'm not working, and I just start eating. And while I'm doing it, I'm not thinking, "Oh, this is delicious." I'm thinking, "Why am I doing this? I need to stop." 

It's frantic, you know? It's like a compulsion. There's no joy in it. It's just a mechanical, miserable process. And then, of course, the second it's over, the guilt hits like a ton of bricks. So, no, there's absolutely no pleasure in it. None whatsoever. It's just... it's just something I do that I hate myself for doing.

Diet? Like, going on a diet or something? No, no I haven't really done anything like that. You have to understand, doc, I’ve never been a diet kind of guy. Never in my fifty-nine years. When you’re driving a rig for a living, your diet is whatever hot meal you can grab at a truck stop at two in the morning, or a quick burger at a place that has parking for an eighteen-wheeler. You just eat to keep your own engine running, you know? You don't sit there counting calories or measuring out portions or whatever it is people do. 

I mean, I see these folks on TV or my sister-in-law talking about keto this and fasting that, and it just sounds like a whole lot of fuss that I don't have the patience for. ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Weight gain? Well, you know, it's funny you ask that, because I was just thinking about this the other day when I was trying to put on a pair of jeans that used to fit me just fine before all this back trouble started. I mean, I've never been a small guy, doc. You don't drive a truck for thirty years and stay skinny, right? You're sitting all day, eating diner food, grabbing snacks at the gas station. So I've always had a bit of a gut, a little extra around the middle. That's just part of the job, part of getting older, too. I'm fifty-nine, after all. My metabolism isn't what it was when I was hauling freight in my twenties.

But as for significant weight gain since these... these eating episodes started? You know, honestly, I couldn't tell you for sure. I haven't stepped on a scale in I don't know how long. We have one in the bathroom, my wife bought it a few years ago, one of those digital ones that connects to your phone or whatever, but I never use it. I just never saw the point. I've always judged my weight by how my clothes fit. If the belt needs to go out a notch, well, I know I've put on a few pounds. 

And lately, since I've been stuck at home with this lumbar injury, mostly just moving from the bed to the recliner and back again... I'm wearing sweatpants a lot. You know? They're just more comfortable when your back is throbbing like a bad tooth. And sweatpants, they stretch. They're forgiving. They don't tell you if you've gained five pounds or ten pounds. So, I haven't really noticed a huge difference in how my clothes fit because I'm not wearing my regular work clothes. 

I suppose it's possible I've put on some weight, what with all the pizza and chips and sitting around not getting any exercise. It stands to reason, right? But I haven't actually noticed a significant change. I haven't looked in the mirror and thought, "Whoa, Magin, you've really blown up." It's more just the general feeling of being sluggish and miserable from the back pain and the guilt of the eating. So, no, I can't say I've noticed any significant weight gain, but I also haven't exactly been keeping track, if you know what I mean.

I mean, a really deep, sickening kind of disgust. \n\nI just stare at the mess and think, this isn't me. It’s like I’m not the steady, in-control man I’ve always tried to be, the man I’ve spent my whole life building myself up to be. I’ve always been the one steering the wheel, keeping everything on track, but when I’m sitting there in the aftermath of it all, looking at the sheer amount of empty boxes and what I just did, I just feel completely out of control and ashamed. It just eats at me. I just can't keep sitting there feeling like that anymore, wondering where the guy who had it all together went.\n\nDoctor: How often do these episodes of losing control with food happen?\n\nPatient: Well, see, that’s the thing. It’s... it’s gotten really bad lately. You see, I’ve actually been off the road for a bit. I’ve got this back injury—you know how it is, sitting in that cab for ten, twelve hours a day, feeling every bump on the interstate, hauling gear... eventually, the lower lumbar just says enough is enough. So I’ve been stuck at home on medical leave, and let me tell you, it is driving me absolutely up the wall. I’m a guy who needs a schedule, a route, a destination. Now I’m just staring at the same four walls in my living room, trying not to tweak my back, and I just don't know what to do with myself. \n\nAnd since I’ve been home with this injury, my whole routine is just shot to hell, and that’s when this eating thing really started to just take over my life. I mean, it’s happening several nights most weeks now. I’ll just be sitting in my recliner, trying to ignore the pain and the sheer boredom of not working, and then I just go off the rails. Several nights almost every single week. \n\nHonestly, I’ve been trying to look back and figure out if I’m having any good stretches, but I really can’t think of a single week in these past three months where I didn’t have at least one of those episodes. Not one single week, doc. Three whole months of just... failing at it. I tell myself on Sunday, \"Alright, this week we keep it together, you're the boss here,\" and then by Tuesday or Wednesday, I'm right back in the middle of it, surrounded by empty boxes and wrappers again. It's just constant, and it's exhausting trying to fight it when you're just sitting around the house all day.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you're unable to stop eating once you've started during these episodes?\n\nPatient: Oh, absolutely. That’s... that is exactly it, doc. It’s like, well, let me try to explain how it feels. You see, when I was driving, I had this iron-clad discipline. You have to, right? You’re hauling thousands of pounds of freight, you’ve got logs to keep, weigh stations, strict deadlines. I was always the guy who could just lock in and get the job done, no matter what. I had total control. \n\nBut with this food... once I take that first bite of whatever it is I've dragged into the living room—pizza, chips, a whole box of whatever—it’s like a switch just flips in my brain. Once I start, it feels like that same discipline I had on the road just completely shuts off. It’s just gone. And the crazy part, the part that really makes me feel like I’m losing my mind, is that I’m sitting there, fully aware of what I’m doing. I’ll literally be talking to myself in my head. I’ll be sitting in my recliner, my back throbbing, and I'm telling myself, \"Magin, put the fork down. Magin, you don’t need another bite. Stop doing this.\" I’m practically pleading with myself to just stop. \n\nBut it’s like my body isn't even listening to my brain anymore. Even while I'm telling myself to quit, my hand just keeps going back for more. Over and over, from the box to my mouth, like some kind of machine. I’ll be chewing and swallowing and reaching for the next handful all while my brain is screaming at me to hit the brakes. It’s the most helpless feeling in the world, doc. I’ve never been a helpless guy, you know? I’ve always been the one in the driver's seat. But in those moments... I’m not driving anything. I’m just along for the ride, and I absolutely cannot stop it once it gets going.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel a sense of pleasure or enjoyment during these episodes of losing control with food?\n\nPatient: Pleasure? Enjoyment? No, doc, no. Not at all. I mean, you'd think so, right? You'd think if a guy is sitting there eating a whole pizza and a family-sized bag of chips, he must be having the time of his life. But it's not like that. It's... it's almost the opposite. \n\nIt's not about tasting the food or savoring it or any of that. When I was on the road, sometimes I'd stop at this diner off I-80, get a hot roast beef sandwich, and man, I'd enjoy that. I'd sit there, take my time, taste the gravy... that was enjoyment. But this? This thing that happens in my living room? There's no enjoyment in it. \n\nHonestly, I don't even think I taste the food half the time. It's just... it's just shoveling it in. It's like I'm trying to fill a hole or just numb out the boredom and the frustration of this damn back injury. I'm sitting there, my back is aching, I'm miserable because I'm not working, and I just start eating. And while I'm doing it, I'm not thinking, \"Oh, this is delicious.\" I'm thinking, \"Why am I doing this? I need to stop.\" \n\nIt's frantic, you know? It's like a compulsion. There's no joy in it. It's just a mechanical, miserable process. And then, of course, the second it's over, the guilt hits like a ton of bricks. So, no, there's absolutely no pleasure in it. None whatsoever. It's just... it's just something I do that I hate myself for doing.\n\nDoctor: Have you tried to diet or restrict your food intake in an attempt to prevent these episodes?\n\nPatient: Diet? Like, going on a diet or something? No, no I haven't really done anything like that. You have to understand, doc, I’ve never been a diet kind of guy. Never in my fifty-nine years. When you’re driving a rig for a living, your diet is whatever hot meal you can grab at a truck stop at two in the morning, or a quick burger at a place that has parking for an eighteen-wheeler. You just eat to keep your own engine running, you know? You don't sit there counting calories or measuring out portions or whatever it is people do. \n\nI mean, I see these folks on TV or my sister-in-law talking about keto this and fasting that, and it just sounds like a whole lot of fuss that I don't have the patience for. So, no, I haven't tried to restrict my food or starve myself during the day to stop what happens at night. I wouldn't even know how to stick to a diet plan anyway, especially now that I'm just sitting around the house all day with this busted lumbar, going stir-crazy. \n\nI just wake up every morning and tell myself I'm going to eat normally today. Just, you know, regular meals. A normal turkey sandwich for lunch, a regular plate of whatever for dinner. I don't try to skip meals or cut out carbs or anything like that. I just want to eat my regular food like a normal guy and be done with it. But then the evening rolls around, and I'm stuck in that recliner, and the boredom and the back pain start creeping in, and... well, you know the rest. I just go off the deep end. But as far as actually going on a diet or purposefully restricting what I eat to try and prevent it from happening? No, I haven't tried that at all.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any significant weight gain since these episodes of losing control with food started happening more frequently?\n\nPatient: Weight gain? My metabolism isn't what it was when I was hauling freight in my twenties.\n\nBut as for significant weight gain since these... these eating episodes started? I've always judged my weight by how my clothes fit. I'm wearing sweatpants a lot. You know? They're just more comfortable when your back is throbbing like a bad tooth. And sweatpants, they stretch. They're forgiving. They don't tell you if you've gained five pounds or ten pounds. My back is still aching, but now my stomach is stretched tight and uncomfortable, and I just... I look at the coffee table. \n\nI sit there looking at all the empty containers. You can't lose your cool. You have to be the guy who handles things, the guy who provides, the guy who keeps his truck on the road and gets the job done safely. That’s who I’ve always tried to be my whole life. A man in control. \n\nBut then I have these nights in my living room, and I'm looking at this pile of empty food containers that I just shoveled into my mouth like I was starving to death, and I realize I have absolutely no control at all. ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Emotions right before? Well... you know, that's a good question. It's not like I'm sitting there thinking, "Oh, I'm feeling sad, I think I'll go eat a whole pizza." It doesn't really work like that for me. It's more of a... a build-up, I guess you could say. 

See, I spend most of my day just sitting in that recliner because of my back. And when you're used to being on the move, driving ten, twelve hours a day, seeing different parts of the country, having a purpose... suddenly being stuck in one room, staring at the same four walls, it does something to your head. You start thinking too much. My mind just goes in circles. I think about my back, wondering if it's ever going to heal right, wondering if I'll ever get back in the cab of my truck. I think about the bills piling up, because disability pay only goes so far, you know? And my wife, she's working extra shifts at the diner just to keep our heads above water, and that makes me feel like a lousy provider, which, like I told you, is a big deal to me. 

So, it's this constant churning of worry and frustration and just... feeling useless. I guess you could call that an emotion, right? That feeling of being totally useless and stuck. And then, usually around the evening, when the house is quiet and my wife is at work and the pain medicine is starting to wear off a little bit, but not enough for me to take the next dose yet... that's when it usually hits. 

It's almost like a pressure cooker. The worry and the physical pain from the lumbar injury, it all just builds and builds until I feel like I'm crawling out of my own skin. I get this restless feeling. I can't get comfortable in the chair, I can't concentrate on the TV, I can't read a book. My mind is just racing, and my back is throbbing, and I just need... I need something to make it all stop for a minute. I need some kind of relief, some kind of distraction. 

And that's when I start thinking about the food. It's not a specific emotion like anger or sadness, it's more like this overwhelming need to just numb everything out. To shut my brain off and give myself a break from the pain and the worrying about the future. But if you're asking if there's one specific feeling I can put my finger on right before I start eating like that? Honestly, doc, I'm not really sure. It's just a whole mess of feeling awful, physically and mentally, and just wanting an escape. I don't know if that makes any sense, but that's the best way I can describe it. It's just this intense build-up of misery until I finally just give in and head for the kitchen.

I had total control. \n\nBut with this food... once I take that first bite of whatever it is I've dragged into the living room—pizza, chips, a whole box of whatever—it’s like a switch just flips in my brain. Once I start, it feels like that same discipline I had on the road just completely shuts off. It’s just gone. And the crazy part, the part that really makes me feel like I’m losing my mind, is that I’m sitting there, fully aware of what I’m doing. I’ll literally be talking to myself in my head. I’ll be sitting in my recliner, my back throbbing, and I'm telling myself, \"Magin, put the fork down. Magin, you don’t need another bite. Stop doing this.\" I’m practically pleading with myself to just stop. \n\nBut it’s like my body isn't even listening to my brain anymore. Even while I'm telling myself to quit, my hand just keeps going back for more. Over and over, from the box to my mouth, like some kind of machine. I’ll be chewing and swallowing and reaching for the next handful all while my brain is screaming at me to hit the brakes. It’s the most helpless feeling in the world, doc. I’ve never been a helpless guy, you know? I’ve always been the one in the driver's seat. But in those moments... I’m not driving anything. I’m just along for the ride, and I absolutely cannot stop it once it gets going.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel a sense of pleasure or enjoyment during these episodes of losing control with food?\n\nPatient: Pleasure? Enjoyment? No, doc, no. Not at all. I mean, you'd think so, right? You'd think if a guy is sitting there eating a whole pizza and a family-sized bag of chips, he must be having the time of his life. But it's not like that. It's... it's almost the opposite. \n\nIt's not about tasting the food or savoring it or any of that. When I was on the road, sometimes I'd stop at this diner off I-80, get a hot roast beef sandwich, and man, I'd enjoy that. I'd sit there, take my time, taste the gravy... that was enjoyment. But this? This thing that happens in my living room? There's no enjoyment in it. \n\nHonestly, I don't even think I taste the food half the time. It's just... it's just shoveling it in. It's like I'm trying to fill a hole or just numb out the boredom and the frustration of this damn back injury. I'm sitting there, my back is aching, I'm miserable because I'm not working, and I just start eating. And while I'm doing it, I'm not thinking, \"Oh, this is delicious.\" I'm thinking, \"Why am I doing this? I need to stop.\" \n\nIt's frantic, you know? It's like a compulsion. There's no joy in it. It's just a mechanical, miserable process. And then, of course, the second it's over, the guilt hits like a ton of bricks. So, no, there's absolutely no pleasure in it. None whatsoever. It's just... it's just something I do that I hate myself for doing.\n\nDoctor: Have you tried to diet or restrict your food intake in an attempt to prevent these episodes?\n\nPatient: Diet? Like, going on a diet or something? No, no I haven't really done anything like that. You have to understand, doc, I’ve never been a diet kind of guy. Never in my fifty-nine years. When you’re driving a rig for a living, your diet is whatever hot meal you can grab at a truck stop at two in the morning, or a quick burger at a place that has parking for an eighteen-wheeler. You just eat to keep your own engine running, you know? You don't sit there counting calories or measuring out portions or whatever it is people do. \n\nI mean, I see these folks on TV or my sister-in-law talking about keto this and fasting that, and it just sounds like a whole lot of fuss that I don't have the patience for. So, no, I haven't tried to restrict my food or starve myself during the day to stop what happens at night. I wouldn't even know how to stick to a diet plan anyway, especially now that I'm just sitting around the house all day with this busted lumbar, going stir-crazy. \n\nI just wake up every morning and tell myself I'm going to eat normally today. Just, you know, regular meals. A normal turkey sandwich for lunch, a regular plate of whatever for dinner. I don't try to skip meals or cut out carbs or anything like that. I just want to eat my regular food like a normal guy and be done with it. But then the evening rolls around, and I'm stuck in that recliner, and the boredom and the back pain start creeping in, and... well, you know the rest. I just go off the deep end. But as far as actually going on a diet or purposefully restricting what I eat to try and prevent it from happening? No, I haven't tried that at all.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any significant weight gain since these episodes of losing control with food started happening more frequently?\n\nPatient: Weight gain? Well, you know, it's funny you ask that, because I was just thinking about this the other day when I was trying to put on a pair of jeans that used to fit me just fine before all this back trouble started. I mean, I've never been a small guy, doc. You don't drive a truck for thirty years and stay skinny, right? You're sitting all day, eating diner food, grabbing snacks at the gas station. So I've always had a bit of a gut, a little extra around the middle. That's just part of the job, part of getting older, too. I'm fifty-nine, after all. My metabolism isn't what it was when I was hauling freight in my twenties.\n\nBut as for significant weight gain since these... these eating episodes started? You know, honestly, I couldn't tell you for sure. I haven't stepped on a scale in I don't know how long. We have one in the bathroom, my wife bought it a few years ago, one of those digital ones that connects to your phone or whatever, but I never use it. I just never saw the point. I've always judged my weight by how my clothes fit. If the belt needs to go out a notch, well, I know I've put on a few pounds. \n\nAnd lately, since I've been stuck at home with this lumbar injury, mostly just moving from the bed to the recliner and back again... I'm wearing sweatpants a lot. You know? They're just more comfortable when your back is throbbing like a bad tooth. And sweatpants, they stretch. They're forgiving. They don't tell you if you've gained five pounds or ten pounds. So, I haven't really noticed a huge difference in how my clothes fit because I'm not wearing my regular work clothes. \n\nI suppose it's possible I've put on some weight, what with all the pizza and chips and sitting around not getting any exercise. It stands to reason, right? But I haven't actually noticed a significant change. I haven't looked in the mirror and thought, \"Whoa, Magin, you've really blown up.\" It's more just the general feeling of being sluggish and miserable from the back pain and the guilt of the eating. So, no, I can't say I've noticed any significant weight gain, but I also haven't exactly been keeping track, if you know what I mean.\n\nDoctor: Do you always feel guilty after these episodes of losing control with food?\n\nPatient: Guilty? Yeah. Yeah, every single time. Honestly, doc, it's... it's the main reason I’m even sitting here talking to you today. What brings me in is that aftermath, you know? The part right after I finally stop eating. The fog kind of lifts, or that frantic feeling finally burns itself out, and I’m just sitting there in my recliner. My back is still aching, but now my stomach is stretched tight and uncomfortable, and I just... I look at the coffee table. \n\nI sit there looking at all the empty containers. A greasy pizza box, a giant bag of chips just completely crumpled up, maybe some empty wrappers... just a whole graveyard of junk. And staring at that mess, the guilt just hits me like a freight train. But it's more than just guilt, really. I feel completely disgusted with myself. I mean, profoundly disgusted. I look at my hands, I look at the garbage, and I just think, \"What the hell is wrong with you?\"\n\nBecause, see, I’ve always been a steady guy. I’ve always prided myself on being an in-control man. You have to be, right? When you’re behind the wheel of a rig, hauling eighty thousand pounds of freight down a steep mountain grade in the pouring rain, you have to be steady. You can't lose your cool. You have to be the guy who handles things, the guy who provides, the guy who keeps his truck on the road and gets the job done safely. That’s who I’ve always tried to be my whole life. A man in control. \n\nBut then I have these nights in my living room, and I'm looking at this pile of empty food containers that I just shoveled into my mouth like I was starving to death, and I realize I have absolutely no control at all. None. A grown man, fifty-nine years old, and I can't even stop myself from eating until I'm sick. It just strips away all your dignity, you know? It makes you feel pathetic. So, yeah, guilty is a good word for it, but that disgust... that feeling of not being the steady man I thought I was... that's the part that really eats at me. That's the part I just can't live with anymore, and why I finally decided I had to come talk to somebody.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever tried to make up for these episodes of overeating by purging or using laxatives?\n\nPatient: Purging? You mean, like... making myself throw up? Oh, Lord, no. No, no, I haven't ever done anything like that. I'll be honest with you, doc, I absolutely hate throwing up. I haven't been sick like that since I got a hold of some bad meatloaf at a diner just outside of Memphis back in, oh, it must have been '98 or '99. It was a miserable experience, being sick in the cab of a truck. Just awful. So the idea of doing that on purpose? Sticking my fingers down my throat after eating? I just couldn't do it. My stomach turns just thinking about it. \n\nAnd laxatives? No way. Absolutely not. See, when you're driving a rig for a living, the very last thing you want to do is mess around with your digestion. You're out on the interstate, sometimes you're thirty, forty miles between rest stops, and you've got a schedule to keep. You can't be taking pills that are going to make you have to run to the bathroom at a moment's notice. You'd be asking for a disaster. It's just ingrained in me to leave my stomach alone. \n\nAnd even now, you know, being stuck at home with this busted lumbar... it's the same principle, really. Getting up out of that recliner is a whole ordeal right now. It takes me a good three or four minutes just to stand up straight, get my balance, and let the shooting pain down my leg subside enough to walk. If I took a laxative and had to make a mad dash for the toilet? Forget about it. I'd probably end up on the floor in absolute agony, or I wouldn't make it in time. \n\nSo, no, I don't do any of that to try and make up for what I ate. Like I was saying before, I just sit there. I sit there in my chair, looking at the empty pizza boxes and chip bags, and my stomach feels like a blown-up balloon. It's stretched so tight it physically hurts, just this heavy, miserable rock in my gut. But I just suffer through it. I sit there with the physical pain of being that full, and the emotional pain of knowing I did it to myself again. I don't try to undo it or cheat my way out of it by getting sick. I just take it, as awful as it feels.\n\nDoctor: Are there any specific emotions or feelings that you notice right before you lose control with food?\n\nPatient: Emotions right before? Well... you know, that's a good question. It's not like I'm sitting there thinking, \"Oh, I'm feeling sad, I think I'll go eat a whole pizza.\" It doesn't really work like that for me. It's more of a... a build-up, I guess you could say. \n\nSee, I spend most of my day just sitting in that recliner because of my back. And when you're used to being on the move, driving ten, twelve hours a day, seeing different parts of the country, having a purpose... suddenly being stuck in one room, staring at the same four walls, it does something to your head. You start thinking too much. My mind just goes in circles. I think about my back, wondering if it's ever going to heal right, wondering if I'll ever get back in the cab of my truck. I think about the bills piling up, because disability pay only goes so far, you know? And my wife, she's working extra shifts at the diner just to keep our heads above water, and that makes me feel like a lousy provider, which, like I told you, is a big deal to me. \n\nSo, it's this constant churning of worry and frustration and just... feeling useless. I guess you could call that an emotion, right? That feeling of being totally useless and stuck. And then, usually around the evening, when the house is quiet and my wife is at work and the pain medicine is starting to wear off a little bit, but not enough for me to take the next dose yet... that's when it usually hits. \n\nIt's almost like a pressure cooker. The worry and the physical pain from the lumbar injury, it all just builds and builds until I feel like I'm crawling out of my own skin. I get this restless feeling. I can't get comfortable in the chair, I can't concentrate on the TV, I can't read a book. My mind is just racing, and my back is throbbing, and I just need... I need something to make it all stop for a minute. I need some kind of relief, some kind of distraction. \n\nAnd that's when I start thinking about the food. It's not a specific emotion like anger or sadness, it's more like this overwhelming need to just numb everything out. To shut my brain off and give myself a break from the pain and the worrying about the future. Well, with my wife... it’s tough. Like I said, she’s working those extra shifts at the diner, bless her heart, and I’m at home. I try my hardest to hide the evidence, you know? Physical health problems? From the eating? Well... no, not that I know of. I mean, obviously, there's my back. That lumbar injury is the whole reason I'm in this mess, sitting in that chair all day. But as far as the food causing new medical problems... no, I haven't really had anything like that pop up. 

You know, it's actually kind of surprising, because in my line of work, you see a lot of guys go down with health issues. Trucking is notoriously hard on the body. You got guys out there with sky-high blood pressure, diabetes, sleep apnea... you name it. They live off truck stop roller-grill hot dogs and giant energy drinks, and by the time they're my age, their bodies are just giving out. But I was never really like that on the road. I always tried to keep myself in decent shape, considering the job. I'd pack a cooler, try to walk a few laps around the rig when I stopped for fuel. 

So, since this whole... eating thing started, I haven't really noticed any new physical conditions. I mean, sure, right after I put away all that food, my stomach is in absolute knots. I get the heartburn, the indigestion, that awful feeling like you've swallowed a bowling ball and you can't even lean back in the recliner without feeling it right up in your chest. Like I said before, my stomach will just ache. But that usually passes by the next morning. 

As far as actual, you know, doctor-diagnosed health problems? Nothing. My blood pressure was fine the last time the workers' comp doctor checked it. They always run my vitals when I go in for the physical therapy assessments for my back—which, by the way, feels like a waste of time lately since the physical therapy doesn't seem to be making a dent in the pain—but anyway, the nurses take my vitals, and nobody has said a word about my sugar or my heart or anything like that. 

I definitely feel my clothes fitting tighter, which is frustrating in its own right. Having to use the next notch on the belt when you're used to being at a steady weight your whole adult life, it really messes with your head. But no actual health problems from it. Just the back. I guess I'm lucky in that regard, all things considered. If I started having heart problems or something on top of the lumbar injury, I don't know what my wife would do. She's already got enough on her plate with those double shifts at the diner. So, yeah, thankfully, physically, it's just the back that's broken.

So, no, I can't say I've noticed any significant weight gain, but I also haven't exactly been keeping track, if you know what I mean.\n\nDoctor: Do you always feel guilty after these episodes of losing control with food?\n\nPatient: Guilty? Yeah. Yeah, every single time. Honestly, doc, it's... it's the main reason I’m even sitting here talking to you today. What brings me in is that aftermath, you know? The part right after I finally stop eating. The fog kind of lifts, or that frantic feeling finally burns itself out, and I’m just sitting there in my recliner. My back is still aching, but now my stomach is stretched tight and uncomfortable, and I just... I look at the coffee table. \n\nI sit there looking at all the empty containers. A greasy pizza box, a giant bag of chips just completely crumpled up, maybe some empty wrappers... just a whole graveyard of junk. And staring at that mess, the guilt just hits me like a freight train. But it's more than just guilt, really. I feel completely disgusted with myself. I mean, profoundly disgusted. I look at my hands, I look at the garbage, and I just think, \"What the hell is wrong with you?\"\n\nBecause, see, I’ve always been a steady guy. I’ve always prided myself on being an in-control man. You have to be, right? When you’re behind the wheel of a rig, hauling eighty thousand pounds of freight down a steep mountain grade in the pouring rain, you have to be steady. You can't lose your cool. You have to be the guy who handles things, the guy who provides, the guy who keeps his truck on the road and gets the job done safely. That’s who I’ve always tried to be my whole life. A man in control. \n\nBut then I have these nights in my living room, and I'm looking at this pile of empty food containers that I just shoveled into my mouth like I was starving to death, and I realize I have absolutely no control at all. None. A grown man, fifty-nine years old, and I can't even stop myself from eating until I'm sick. It just strips away all your dignity, you know? It makes you feel pathetic. So, yeah, guilty is a good word for it, but that disgust... that feeling of not being the steady man I thought I was... that's the part that really eats at me. That's the part I just can't live with anymore, and why I finally decided I had to come talk to somebody.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever tried to make up for these episodes of overeating by purging or using laxatives?\n\nPatient: Purging? You mean, like... making myself throw up? Oh, Lord, no. No, no, I haven't ever done anything like that. I'll be honest with you, doc, I absolutely hate throwing up. I haven't been sick like that since I got a hold of some bad meatloaf at a diner just outside of Memphis back in, oh, it must have been '98 or '99. It was a miserable experience, being sick in the cab of a truck. Just awful. So the idea of doing that on purpose? Sticking my fingers down my throat after eating? I just couldn't do it. My stomach turns just thinking about it. \n\nAnd laxatives? No way. Absolutely not. See, when you're driving a rig for a living, the very last thing you want to do is mess around with your digestion. You're out on the interstate, sometimes you're thirty, forty miles between rest stops, and you've got a schedule to keep. You can't be taking pills that are going to make you have to run to the bathroom at a moment's notice. You'd be asking for a disaster. It's just ingrained in me to leave my stomach alone. \n\nAnd even now, you know, being stuck at home with this busted lumbar... it's the same principle, really. Getting up out of that recliner is a whole ordeal right now. It takes me a good three or four minutes just to stand up straight, get my balance, and let the shooting pain down my leg subside enough to walk. If I took a laxative and had to make a mad dash for the toilet? Forget about it. I'd probably end up on the floor in absolute agony, or I wouldn't make it in time. \n\nSo, no, I don't do any of that to try and make up for what I ate. Like I was saying before, I just sit there. I sit there in my chair, looking at the empty pizza boxes and chip bags, and my stomach feels like a blown-up balloon. It's stretched so tight it physically hurts, just this heavy, miserable rock in my gut. But I just suffer through it. I sit there with the physical pain of being that full, and the emotional pain of knowing I did it to myself again. I don't try to undo it or cheat my way out of it by getting sick. I just take it, as awful as it feels.\n\nDoctor: Are there any specific emotions or feelings that you notice right before you lose control with food?\n\nPatient: Emotions right before? Well... you know, that's a good question. It's not like I'm sitting there thinking, \"Oh, I'm feeling sad, I think I'll go eat a whole pizza.\" It doesn't really work like that for me. It's more of a... a build-up, I guess you could say. \n\nSee, I spend most of my day just sitting in that recliner because of my back. And when you're used to being on the move, driving ten, twelve hours a day, seeing different parts of the country, having a purpose... suddenly being stuck in one room, staring at the same four walls, it does something to your head. You start thinking too much. My mind just goes in circles. I think about my back, wondering if it's ever going to heal right, wondering if I'll ever get back in the cab of my truck. I think about the bills piling up, because disability pay only goes so far, you know? And my wife, she's working extra shifts at the diner just to keep our heads above water, and that makes me feel like a lousy provider, which, like I told you, is a big deal to me. \n\nSo, it's this constant churning of worry and frustration and just... feeling useless. I guess you could call that an emotion, right? That feeling of being totally useless and stuck. And then, usually around the evening, when the house is quiet and my wife is at work and the pain medicine is starting to wear off a little bit, but not enough for me to take the next dose yet... that's when it usually hits. \n\nIt's almost like a pressure cooker. The worry and the physical pain from the lumbar injury, it all just builds and builds until I feel like I'm crawling out of my own skin. I get this restless feeling. I can't get comfortable in the chair, I can't concentrate on the TV, I can't read a book. My mind is just racing, and my back is throbbing, and I just need... I need something to make it all stop for a minute. I need some kind of relief, some kind of distraction. \n\nAnd that's when I start thinking about the food. It's not a specific emotion like anger or sadness, it's more like this overwhelming need to just numb everything out. To shut my brain off and give myself a break from the pain and the worrying about the future. But if you're asking if there's one specific feeling I can put my finger on right before I start eating like that? Honestly, doc, I'm not really sure. It's just a whole mess of feeling awful, physically and mentally, and just wanting an escape. I don't know if that makes any sense, but that's the best way I can describe it. It's just this intense build-up of misery until I finally just give in and head for the kitchen.\n\nDoctor: Have you had any problems with your relationships, such as with your wife, because of these episodes of losing control with food?\n\nPatient: Well, with my wife... it’s tough. Like I said, she’s working those extra shifts at the diner, bless her heart, and I’m at home. I try my hardest to hide the evidence, you know? I’ll gather up all the wrappers and the greasy boxes, and I’ll take them out to the outside bin in the dead of night. I'll even bury them under the regular household trash so she doesn't see just how much I actually put away. But you can’t hide something like this forever. She knows. She doesn't yell or anything, but there's this... this heavy silence between us sometimes. I catch her looking at me with this mix of worry and, I don't know, maybe pity? And for a man who’s supposed to be the provider, seeing pity in your wife’s eyes... it just guts you. It really does. It puts a wall right down the middle of our living room.\n\nBut honestly, doc, it’s not just my marriage. It’s bleeding into my other relationships, too. Especially with the guys from work. See, before this lumbar thing laid me up, I was one of the senior drivers at the company. I had this whole roster of younger guys, rookies fresh out of CDL school, that the dispatcher had me mentoring. You know how it is, these kids get out on the interstate and they think they know everything, but they don’t know the first thing about managing a logbook, or how to handle an eighty-thousand-pound rig when the crosswinds kick up in Wyoming. So I was their guy. I’d do these weekly check-in calls, give them advice, keep them steady. \n\nBut lately? I can’t do it. I’ve started completely avoiding their check-in calls. I’ll see their names pop up on my caller ID, and I just sit there in my chair and watch the phone ring. I just let it go straight to voicemail. And it’s because... I just feel so ashamed. How am I supposed to get on the phone and lecture a twenty-two-year-old kid about discipline and keeping a strict routine on the road, when I’m sitting here completely out of control? I don’t want anyone hearing my voice and figuring out how far off my routine I’ve gotten. I don't want them to know that the steady, reliable mentor they look up to is spending his nights shoveling junk food into his mouth until his stomach hurts. So I just cut them off. I isolate myself. I'm letting down my wife, I'm letting down those kids I'm supposed to be guiding... it's just a mess. A real mess.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever felt so down or depressed that you thought you'd be better off dead?\n\nPatient: Better off dead? Oh, Lord, no. No, doc, it hasn't ever gotten to that point. I mean... don't get me wrong, I get down. I get real down. You sit in a recliner all day, day in and day out, staring at the dust motes floating in the sunlight and feeling your gut ache from whatever you shoved into it the night before... well, you're gonna feel pretty low. It’s a dark place to be in, sitting there feeling like a failure while your wife is out busting her hump just to keep the lights on. \n\nBut dead? No. I've never thought that. See, I still got my wife to think about, for one thing. If I were to just... check out, who's gonna take care of her? She's already pulling those double shifts at the diner, coming home smelling like fry grease and looking so tired she can barely keep her eyes open. If I were gone, she'd be left with all the bills, the mortgage, funeral costs... I couldn't do that to her. I couldn't live with myself—or, well, you know what I mean. I couldn't do that to her.\n\nAnd besides all that, I still have this... this hope, I guess you'd call it. I keep holding onto the idea that maybe this lumbar thing will finally heal up right. I spend half my day just picturing myself climbing back up into the cab of a rig, feeling that big diesel engine rumble right up through the seat, hitting the open interstate with the sun coming up over the dashboard. I miss that life so much it physically hurts my chest just talking about it. I want to get back to it. I don't want to just give up and be put in the ground. \n\nSo, yeah, I get depressed. I get so frustrated with myself and this whole situation that sometimes I just sit there and my eyes well up, just out of sheer helplessness. I just want to fix this mess. I want to get my life back to the way it was before everything went off the rails.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any physical health problems that you think might be related to these episodes of overeating?\n\nPatient: Physical health problems? But as far as the food causing new medical problems... no, I haven't really had anything like that pop up. \n\nYou know, it's actually kind of surprising, because in my line of work, you see a lot of guys go down with health issues. They live off truck stop roller-grill hot dogs and giant energy drinks, and by the time they're my age, their bodies are just giving out. But I was never really like that on the road. I always tried to keep myself in decent shape, considering the job. Sleep patterns? Hmm. Well, you know, sleep is... it's a funny thing when you've been a trucker for as long as I have. You get used to sleeping anywhere, anytime, under just about any conditions. Weight? Gained a lot of weight? Well, you know, it’s a fair question. Honestly, anybody looking at what I’m doing in the kitchen at midnight would ask the exact same thing. It's a whole bureaucratic headache that can cost you your livelihood. So for the last thirty years, I’ve always kept a pretty close eye on where I stand, weight-wise. 

Now, since this lumbar thing put me out of commission and stuck me in that recliner, and especially with these... well, with the sheer volume of food I'm putting away when I lose control... Well... you know, that's a good question. It's not like I'm sitting there thinking, \"Oh, I'm feeling sad, I think I'll go eat a whole pizza.\" It doesn't really work like that for me. It's more of a... a build-up, I guess you could say. \n\nSee, I spend most of my day just sitting in that recliner because of my back. And when you're used to being on the move, driving ten, twelve hours a day, seeing different parts of the country, having a purpose... suddenly being stuck in one room, staring at the same four walls, it does something to your head. You start thinking too much. My mind just goes in circles. I think about my back, wondering if it's ever going to heal right, wondering if I'll ever get back in the cab of my truck. I think about the bills piling up, because disability pay only goes so far, you know? And my wife, she's working extra shifts at the diner just to keep our heads above water, and that makes me feel like a lousy provider, which, like I told you, is a big deal to me. \n\nSo, it's this constant churning of worry and frustration and just... feeling useless. I guess you could call that an emotion, right? That feeling of being totally useless and stuck. The worry and the physical pain from the lumbar injury, it all just builds and builds until I feel like I'm crawling out of my own skin. I get this restless feeling. I can't get comfortable in the chair, I can't concentrate on the TV, I can't read a book. My mind is just racing, and my back is throbbing, and I just need... It's just this intense build-up of misery until I finally just give in and head for the kitchen.\n\nDoctor: Have you had any problems with your relationships, such as with your wife, because of these episodes of losing control with food?\n\nPatient: Well, with my wife... it’s tough.
